title: Checkpoint: Atoms
objective: After this level you can describe the parts of an atom and how we discovered them.
summary: Electrons don't orbit like planets: since Schrodinger (1926) they are clouds in orbitals, regions where they are most likely found. One timeline holds the chapter, from Democritus to the neutron.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: the atom keeps getting redrawn.
cards.body: Every new experiment forced a new sketch. Here is the latest update, and then the whole chapter as one timeline.

cards.headline: From orbits to clouds
cards.body: Level 14's shells are a useful picture, but electrons don't circle the nucleus like planets around the Sun. In 1926, Erwin Schrödinger described electrons as waves. Today an electron's home is an orbital: a region where it is most likely to be found. Shells survive as the layers where those clouds sit. The modern atom is a tiny nucleus wrapped in fuzzy electron clouds.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: electrons don't orbit like planets. Picture clouds where they're likely to be.

cards.headline: Every picture earned its place
cards.body: Notice the pattern. Each model lasted until an experiment broke it: cathode rays cracked the uncuttable atom, and gold foil sank the plum pudding. The atom itself never changed. Our picture of it did, one experiment at a time.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: How the atom went from an uncuttable Greek idea to a tiny nucleus wrapped in electron clouds.
Why an atom is mostly empty space, yet nearly all its mass sits in its tiny nucleus.
Why the outer electrons, not the neutrons, decide how an atom behaves.
How radioactive decay and half-life let carbon-14 date things that were once alive.

questions.prompt: In today's model of the atom, what is an orbital?

options.label: A fixed circle an electron travels around
options.rationale: That is the old planet-like picture.

options.label: A particle inside the nucleus
options.rationale: Orbitals are about electrons, outside the nucleus.

options.label: A region where an electron is most likely found
The empty space between two atoms
options.rationale: An orbital belongs to one atom's electrons.

questions.explanation: An orbital is a region of the atom where an electron is most likely to be found.

questions.prompt: Atoms recap: how does the 1926 picture of electrons differ from simple planet-like orbits?

options.label: Electrons became particles inside the nucleus
Electrons are waves spread in clouds, not circling planets
Electrons were found to have no charge
Shells were abolished completely
options.rationale: Shells survive as layers where the clouds sit.

questions.explanation: Schrodinger described electrons as waves. They occupy orbitals, cloud-like regions, rather than planet-like paths.

questions.prompt: Atoms recap: carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon. Which particle count do they share?

options.label: Nothing at all
options.rationale: Their protons match, which is why both are carbon.

questions.explanation: Every carbon atom has 6 protons. The isotopes differ only in neutrons.

questions.prompt: Atoms recap: Becquerel's fogged plates and carbon dating both depend on which process?

options.label: Electrons filling their shells
options.rationale: Shell-filling doesn't fog plates or tell time.

options.label: Metals rusting in air
options.rationale: Rusting is a chemical change, not a nuclear one.

options.label: Light bouncing off atoms
options.rationale: Both involve radiation from nuclei, not reflected light.

questions.explanation: Uranium's decay fogged Becquerel's plates, and carbon-14's steady decay is the clock in carbon dating.

questions.prompt: Atoms recap: which discovery first showed that the Greeks' "uncuttable" atom had smaller parts?

options.label: Becquerel's radioactivity in 1896
options.rationale: That showed nuclei can decay; the first part found was the electron.

questions.explanation: Thomson found particles far lighter than any atom, inside all matter: the atom had a piece you could knock off.
